title: Precise and Wrong: What Averaging Cannot Fix

questions.question: A sensor's readings scatter by 5 cm and sit 27 cm away from the truth. You average a million of them. What do you get?
options: A very steady reading that is still 27 cm wrong
A reading accurate to well under a millimetre
A reading accurate to about 5 cm
The same answer as one reading
questions.explanation: Measured: 10.3132 from one reading, 10.2700 from a million, against a truth of 10. Past about a hundred samples nothing further happens, because there is nothing left to average away.

questions.question: You zero a rangefinder at 10 m and it is exact there. In use it reads 15 cm long at 0 m and 15 cm short at 20 m. What is wrong?
options: A scale error that an offset was asked to fix, so one reference could never have caught it
The zeroing was done carelessly and should be repeated
The sensor is not linear and needs a curve
Noise, which needs a longer filter
questions.explanation: Wrong at both ends by the same amount in opposite directions is the signature of a scale error. Wrong by the same amount everywhere is an offset; wrong in the same direction at both ends is a bend.

questions.question: Your five calibration references all happen to read the same raw value. The least squares fit divides by zero. Why is the resulting nan worse than a wrong number?
options: Because every comparison against a nan is false, so a check written as a list of values to reject passes it through
Because a nan crashes the program at the point it is produced
Because it prints as -nan, which is confusing
Because the numerator is also zero
questions.explanation: (v < 0.0 || v > 100.0) lets the nan through; !(v >= 0.0 && v <= 100.0) catches it. The two say the same thing in English. Phrase the condition as what you require, then negate it.

questions.question: The datasheet says the sensor reads 0.985 x + 0.42. You store those two numbers as your calibration. What happens?
options: Every reading is about twice as wrong as no calibration at all, in numbers that still look plausible
The readings are exactly correct
The readings are unchanged
The readings are wrong by a constant that is easy to spot
questions.explanation: That line is what the sensor does. The correction is its inverse, 1.0152 raw - 0.4264. Applying the sensor's own line applies the error a second time. Measured: 20 m reads 20.238 instead of 20.120.

questions.question: Two references or a hundred and twenty eight, on a sensor that is genuinely straight. Does the count matter?
options: Yes: the references have their own error, and the fit averages it down. Four times the references, half the error
No: two points determine a line exactly
Yes, but only up to about ten references
Yes: more references make the fit worse by overfitting
questions.explanation: Measured rms error of the resulting calibration: 0.0372 m from two references, 0.0192 from eight, 0.0098 from thirty two, 0.0052 from a hundred and twenty eight. The same square root law as the filter in 15-01.

questions.question: Your fit's rms residual is about the size of the sensor's noise. What have you learned?
options: That the line is as good as the data given, which does not prove the sensor is straight: a bend smaller than the noise leaves no trace
That the sensor is linear
That the calibration is correct to within the noise at every distance
That more references would not help
questions.explanation: The same bend measured 11 percent above the straight sensor's residual at 5 cm of noise and 490 percent above it at 5 mm. The residual finds what the noise does not hide, and the bend is there either way.
